source.publisher: FATF and Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units
source.title: Concealment of Beneficial Ownership

summary: Joint FATF-Egmont Group study analysing 106 case studies on how criminals conceal beneficial ownership of illicit assets. It finds shell companies are the dominant vehicle, usually combined with layered/complex ownership chains across multiple jurisdictions, formal or informal nominee directors/shareholders, trusts and other legal arrangements, bearer shares, and falsified activities (false loans/invoices, manipulated prospectuses). Professional intermediaries -- lawyers, accountants and trust and company service providers (TCSPs) -- feature in most schemes, ranging from unwitting/negligent involvement to full complicity, exploiting weaknesses such as limited AML/CFT obligations for DNFBPs, legal professional privilege, shelf-company sales, directorship/virtual-office services, trust and client accounts, and cross-border service provision. Environmental vulnerabilities include low-tax/offshore jurisdictions, major trade and finance centres, and online/virtual onboarding. The report includes a Horizontal Study of 64 jurisdictions' supervision and enforcement of beneficial ownership obligations, 106 annexed case summaries with tagged red-flag indicators, and a consolidated Annex E list of indicators of concealed beneficial ownership covering client, legal-person/shell-company, and transaction characteristics.

citations.quote: The use of specialists and professional intermediaries, including lawyers, accountants, and TCSPs, is a key feature of the money laundering and broader organised crime environment.
This “continuum of complicity” can be equally applied to all professional intermediary sectors, and is not unique to the legal profession.

extraction_notes: This is a broad, global FATF-Egmont typology report (190pp, 106 case studies + Annex B Horizontal Study of 64 jurisdictions + Annex E consolidated indicator list) rather than a single-incident advisory; typologies and indicators selected above are the most extensively developed themes (layered/complex ownership, shell company networks, nominee/hidden-controller structures, circular/loan-back schemes, and gatekeeper complicity). Jurisdictions list is illustrative of the most frequently cited case-study/offshore jurisdictions, not exhaustive -- the report explicitly declines to name high-risk jurisdictions definitively (para 25, 210). TBML is mentioned only in passing (p.77) and was not extracted as a standalone typology per the narrative-vs-indicator-list rule. Reviewer should confirm whether additional emergent/KC typologies are warranted for 'false loan-back schemes' and 'real estate laundering via professional intermediaries', for which Knowledge Centre searches returned no match but which are supported by multiple case studies (5, 6, 7, 8, 88, 100-104).
